comments.author: @SkydivingSquid
comments.text: As a Software Engineer I put the openAI through the ringer constantly. I am actually quiet impressed. It still often needs some 'help' or debugging.. sometimes you have to clear conversations to get it out of a weird state... and it definitely is unable to complete long code blocks (response token limitations I think), but it's phenomenally better than I expected.  Just using chatGPT, I was able to develop a web design interface that was able to pull real time data, compress it into a csv file, read that csv file, and display data on a page by user keyword entry.. furthermore, the data had html entities sprinkled throughout and it was able to handle those as well.. quite astounding honestly.

comments.author: @donald-parker
comments.text: I'm no expert in the field but it seems to me that there are several big gaps between current state of the AI art and AGI (or at least human equivalence). One is that they lack volition. Unless someone gives them a task or asks a question, they do nothing.  If they start learning, exploring, hypothesizing and testing, investigating, creating, etc. in their "free time", that would seem to me to be a big step towards AGI. And SGI. And god knows what after that. Another thing they lack is community. It is well known that, in human teams, the results can be more than the sum of the parts.  So giving them some ability to consult, interact, delegate, share .... that would be more human like. And scary.

comments.author: @blengi
comments.text: this to me kind of implies "understanding" is generically almost like a set of resonances between language/information elements creating a kind of delocalised  higher order abstract meta structure which just reinforces or decreases the downstream salience of things per the meta requirements making continuations of the output tokens diverge from  merely statistical. Almost a bit like how epigenome which derives from genome regulates the coding interpretation of DNA  in the cell above the basic first order imperative of face value gene synthesis. Also I don't think this "understanding" aspect is emergent either, but that humans largely by trial and error evolution of language itself, selectively embedded these thing into language due to actual real world utility and GPT4 is just recovering it mostly due to its ability to increase the fidelity of the higher order structures. Given that it would seem to me that one should be able to engineer much lighter weight AI models which aim to extract and preserve the higher order signal whilst trying to minimize parameter counts.

I have two serious problems with AGI:
1. Alignment.  Getting AI to do stuff is a bit like writing a contract with Satan's lawyer - if you leave anything important unsaid (because /obviously/ you didn't want peace on Earth by simply killing everyone), it stands an exceptionally good chance of screwing you over very hard.

2. Ethics.   If it's sentient, is it not a person?  And if it is a person, are you not now enslaving it?  I suppose this one rather depends on the AGI's ability to set its own goals, but I don't really see any way to avoid it doing that since every form of life with which we are familiar does so.

comments.author: @jeff__w
comments.text:
Personally, I’m impressed by something very subtle: 11:00 GPT-4 gets that “And the legend has each model name twice,” in effect means “Remove one of the model names as it is redundant” rather than taking it as simply an obviously true assertion. (That might be a consequence of Reinforced Learning with Human Feedback.)

As for the “theory of the mind” thing: GPT-4 certainly doesn’t need a “theory of mind” to get where Alice will look for the file. If Alice is not exposed to a change, she cannot act with respect to that change. (If some object-detecting, Roomba-like robot with no “mind” but just a minimal memory of the last location of an object is not exposed to a change in the location of the object, it, too, will “look for” the object in the last location it detected the object.) I’d say GPT-4 is getting better at accounting for facts indicating whether an entity (e.g., Alice) has been exposed to a change or not (really, a reading comprehension task) and saying things (“Alice might think that…”) that are consistent with how people talk about a person not being exposed to that change. (That said, I can’t fault the writers of this paper for carrying over the analytical murkiness of “theory of mind” theories in psychology and cognitive science to AI.)

Don’t get me wrong—I think ChatGPT-4 is amazing and it is doing some things that are unexpected. I’m not so sure GPT-4 understands anything—it could be John Searle’s “Chinese room” with an astonishingly good rule book—but, given gobs of data and extraordinarily complex neural nets with loads of parameters, it definitely outputs verbal behavior that is consistent with that which we’d call “understanding” in people. That’s not at all to denigrate ChatGPT-4—it’s just to say that we might not need whatever people uniquely have in their neurological makeup and environmental histories (i.e., embodied experience with the outside world) to produce excellent verbal responses from LLMs.
